ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The trapezius is a large superficial back muscle that moves and stabilises the scapula. It is innervated by the spinal accessory nerve and receives proprioceptive input from the cervical plexus.

sections.p: The trapezius spans the posterior neck, upper back and shoulder, forming a diamond‑shaped sheet that connects the occipital bone to the thoracic spine and clavicle.
b: Divided into descending, transverse and ascending fibers
Acts to elevate, retract and rotate the scapula

sections.p: It originates from the external occipital protuberance, nuchal ligament, and spinous processes C7–T12, inserting on the lateral clavicle, acromion and spine of scapula.
b: Visible as a contour on the posterior neck and shoulder

sections.p: Deep to the trapezius lie the levator scapulae and rhomboids; the spinal accessory nerve runs on its surface before piercing it.
b: Posterior triangle of neck contains CN XI and the transverse cervical vessels
Upper fibers overlies the supraclavicular nerves

sections.p: Arterial blood comes from the transverse cervical artery (branch of the thyrocervical trunk) and the dorsal scapular artery.
b: Venous drainage follows the transverse cervical veins to the brachiocephalic vein

sections.p: Motor innervation is via the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); proprioceptive fibers travel with the cervical plexus (C3‑C4).
b: Lesion of CN XI causes shoulder droop and inability to shrug

sections.p: Upper fibers elevate the scapula; middle fibers retract; lower fibers depress and upwardly rotate the scapula during arm elevation.
b: Cooperates with serratus anterior for full overhead reach

sections.p: Weakness or paralysis of the trapezius leads to shoulder droop, winged scapula, and difficulty raising the arm above head. Trauma, neck surgery, or accessory nerve injury are common causes.
b: Accessory nerve palsy: ipsilateral shoulder droop, difficulty shrugging
Spinal accessory nerve stretch in neck dissection
Upper motor neuron lesions produce contralateral trapezius weakness with ipsilateral SCM signs

t.b: Confirms neurogenic loss; absent motor unit potentials indicate nerve injury
Detects compressive lesions (tumor, hematoma) affecting CN XI
Assesses motor function; inability to raise shoulder indicates trapezius weakness

sections.p: Ask the patient to shrug against resistance (trapezius) and turn the head against resistance (sternocleidomastoid) to test CN XI integrity.
b: Upper motor neuron lesion: contralateral trapezius weakness, ipsilateral SCM weakness
Lower motor neuron lesion: isolated ipsilateral trapezius weakness

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden shoulder droop with neck pain after trauma
Associated neurological deficits suggesting spinal cord or brainstem involvement

faq.q: Why does a lesion of the spinal accessory nerve cause shoulder droop?
faq.a: The nerve supplies the trapezius, which lifts the shoulder; loss of this action lets the arm hang.

faq.q: Can a brain stroke affect the trapezius?
faq.a: Yes; a unilateral upper motor neuron lesion can cause contralateral trapezius weakness together with ipsilateral SCM signs.

faq.q: What is the difference between a winged scapula from trapezius vs. serratus anterior?
faq.a: Trapezius weakness causes medial winging with drooping shoulder; serratus anterior loss causes lateral winging with the scapula protruding outward.
